messages.subject: Difference between BRMSEA and RMSEA (in bivariate latent change score model)
parts:
Hi,
I am trying to estimate a bivariate latent change score model that also includes using the change scores as predictors of an outcome. The model converges fine. When comparing the ML estimates and Bayesian posterior means, they are extremely similar.

However, in my model, I have noticed that the estimated (posterior mean) BRMSEA is quite different from the maximum likelihood estimate (.15 instead of .07). This is specific to the BRMSEA and not the same for, eg. BCFI, - there, results are very similiar to the frequentist estimates.

When trying out different models using other data, it also seemed that the BRMSEA is especially sensitive.
How should one deal with such results? I know that the overall posterior is more important than the mean, but for the BRMSEA it seems like the entire distribution is very far from the ML point estimate. Is it because of the type of model used (df=16, N=350)?
Any help or ideas are greatly appreciated!
best
Mischa

parts:
Mischa

Are you using the defaults of the blavFitindices function?
How about the median? Remember that these indices are bounded, so might have hit the boundary and with a very skew distribution the mean would be moved to the tail. You can see an example in the help page on how to plot the posterior to see if that is the case

On a more general comment, I dont recommend the RMSEA in general, because it is sensitve to model type/size. I recommend to use CFI and gamma-hat, as these are less sensitive to things like this


Garnier-Villarreal, M., & Jorgensen, T. D. (2020). Adapting Fit Indices for Bayesian Structural Equation Modeling: Comparison to Maximum Likelihood. Psychological Methods, 25(1), 46–70. https://doi.org/dx.doi.org/10.1037/met0000224

Fan, X., & Sivo, S. A. (2007). Sensitivity of fit indices to model misspecification and model types. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42(3), 509–529. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273170701382864

How about the median? Remember that these indices are bounded, so might have hit the boundary and with a very skew distribution the mean would be moved to the tail. You can see an example in the help page on how to plot the posterior to see if that is the case

On a more general comment, I dont recommend the RMSEA in general, because it is sensitve to model type/size. I recommend to use CFI and gamma-hat, as these are less sensitive to things like this

So, what happens is that RMSEA is a measure of misfit per df. The new method corrects the estimated deviation by the effective number of parameters (pD), and with few df, loo/waic over corrects it in comparosin to the ML models. These differences between pD is not much, and in most common scenarios (larger models) dic is gives the wrong "correction". But in these specific scenarios and just for RMSEA loo/waic corrects more than expected

I just remember another post here, that had a similar issue. When the ML model has low df, this happended.

So, what happens is that RMSEA is a measure of misfit per df. The new method corrects the estimated deviation by the effective number of parameters (pD), and with few df, loo/waic over corrects it in comparosin to the ML models. These differences between pD is not much, and in most common scenarios (larger models) dic is gives the wrong "correction". But in these specific scenarios and just for RMSEA loo/waic corrects more than expected

Hope this helps

How about the median? Remember that these indices are bounded, so might have hit the boundary and with a very skew distribution the mean would be moved to the tail. You can see an example in the help page on how to plot the posterior to see if that is the case

On a more general comment, I dont recommend the RMSEA in general, because it is sensitve to model type/size. I recommend to use CFI and gamma-hat, as these are less sensitive to things like this

I just remember another post here, that had a similar issue. When the ML model has low df, this happended.

So, what happens is that RMSEA is a measure of misfit per df. The new method corrects the estimated deviation by the effective number of parameters (pD), and with few df, loo/waic over corrects it in comparosin to the ML models. These differences between pD is not much, and in most common scenarios (larger models) dic is gives the wrong "correction". But in these specific scenarios and just for RMSEA loo/waic corrects more than expected

I just remember another post here, that had a similar issue. When the ML model has low df, this happended.

So, what happens is that RMSEA is a measure of misfit per df. The new method corrects the estimated deviation by the effective number of parameters (pD), and with few df, loo/waic over corrects it in comparosin to the ML models. These differences between pD is not much, and in most common scenarios (larger models) dic is gives the wrong "correction". But in these specific scenarios and just for RMSEA loo/waic corrects more than expected

Ed and Mischa

I dont think we need more research. Because research has shown consistently that RMSEA is not a great fit index, basically guided by model type and size (df), same conclusion as the one you shared here.

Thats why for overall model fit I recommend SRMR, CFI, and gamma-hat

The idea of model specify cutoffs is interesting, several people have suggested it over time. One of the main reasons to develop the simsem R package, does this very easily. But it leads to similar issues as power analysis. Now you have to define popolation paraemters for the model, and "acceptable misfit" of the model. Whcih can take many forms, and hard to decide in applied reasearch

I just remember another post here, that had a similar issue. When the ML model has low df, this happended.

So, what happens is that RMSEA is a measure of misfit per df. The new method corrects the estimated deviation by the effective number of parameters (pD), and with few df, loo/waic over corrects it in comparosin to the ML models. These differences between pD is not much, and in most common scenarios (larger models) dic is gives the wrong "correction". But in these specific scenarios and just for RMSEA loo/waic corrects more than expected

Hope this helps

On a more general comment, I dont recommend the RMSEA in general, because it is sensitve to model type/size. I recommend to use CFI and gamma-hat, as these are less sensitive to things like this
